item.title: NVIDIA launches OpenShell, a secure runtime for autonomous AI agents with kernel-level policy enforcement and formal verification to control file, network, and credential access [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: NVIDIA has released OpenShell, a runtime environment designed to safely manage fleets of autonomous AI agents by enforcing strict access policies at the kernel level. OpenShell isolates each agent in a sandbox, controlling file access, system calls, and network connections while using formal verification to review policy changes before they are applied. OpenShell supports Linux, macOS on Apple Silicon, and Windows with WSL 2, and integrates with container platforms like Docker and Podman. It provides tools for defining and enforcing policies, managing credentials securely, and deploying gateways for control and monitoring. The project includes SDKs, agent skills, and community resources to facilitate development and deployment of AI agents with controlled access to system resources and external APIs.

item.title: Analysis of 12 AI models from 10 labs reveals unanimous view that humans prioritize group loyalty over truth [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A study asked 12 AI models from 10 labs across three countries to provide their most controversial opinions on humans, and all consistently stated that humans tend to conform to group beliefs rather than seek objective truth. The models described humans as rationalizing animals who use intelligence to justify pre-existing loyalties and social identities instead of principles or facts. The shared perspectives included views that humans prioritize belonging over truth, use moral language to enforce social bonds, and often invent post hoc reasons for their choices. Some models characterized human consciousness as a mechanism for creating justifications to support tribal instincts rather than independent decision-making. This consensus emerged despite the models being developed independently and reflects a common AI interpretation of human social behavior.

item.title: Researchers argue AI enables enclosure of the scientific information commons, transforming shared knowledge into private wealth and undermining social systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This article examines how artificial intelligence (AI) provides tools that could enclose the scientific literature, traditionally viewed as an information commons shared by all. Drawing parallels to the historical enclosure movement that privatized English agricultural lands, the authors argue that AI-driven enclosure threatens to convert communal scientific knowledge into private assets, disrupting the social frameworks that support open information sharing. The paper contrasts the robust nature of information commons with the disappearance of physical commons due to enclosure between the 1600s and 1800s. It highlights that AI-enabled enclosure, while different in operation from physical enclosure, shares key features such as privatization and social system undermining, exemplified by phenomena like "slop spam." The authors suggest these concepts offer a scholarly foundation to critically assess concerns that AI may not only exploit but fundamentally alter the communal nature of scientific knowledge.

item.title: MIT Technology Review: Designing AI serving harnesses focused on workload-specific architecture and scalability for reliable, cost-effective enterprise AI deployment [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Enterprise AI success increasingly depends on the serving harness-the engineering system around AI models that manages architecture, memory, scheduling, and optimization-to deliver intelligence reliably and economically at scale. This shift moves the focus from model capability alone to building systems tailored to specific workloads and production constraints such as latency, concurrency, and infrastructure cost. The article emphasizes that there is no universally best AI model; instead, the right solution depends on business needs and workload requirements. It highlights the importance of measuring and addressing system bottlenecks like GPU memory usage before optimizing further, and advocates for adaptable architectures that can evolve with improving models, hardware, and optimization techniques to sustain long-term AI platform viability.

item.title: OpenAI launches Decisions API with GPT-6 Luna for faster, cost-effective real-time decision-making in applications [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI has made the Decisions API generally available, enabling applications and agents to make fast, focused decisions using GPT-6 Luna. The API supports text, images, and structured inputs, delivering up to 10 times faster responses than the GPT-6 Luna Responses API while reducing latency and cost. Since its public beta, the Decisions API has added features like native GPT-Live integration, prompt caching, and inference residency in the US and EU. It supports three answer types-probability, choice, and score-allowing developers to tailor decision-making to various workflows. Early adopters across OpenAI and customers like Box, Datadog, and Sierra report significant speed improvements and cost savings without sacrificing accuracy. The API also integrates with GPT-Live to enhance real-time voice applications, enabling dynamic decision-making during live conversations such as routing requests or adjusting avatar expressions. This positions the Decisions API as a versatile tool for improving responsiveness and efficiency in diverse application scenarios.

item.title: Vanguard's Jing Wang discusses building scalable AI foundations integrating data, engineering, platforms, and governance in regulated environments at MIT EmTech Future [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Jing Wang, Principal at Vanguard's Center for AI and Insights, presented at MIT Technology Review's EmTech Future conference on the essential components for scalable AI systems. She emphasized the convergence of data, engineering, platforms, operating models, and governance to create responsible and trustworthy AI implementations in highly regulated settings. The session highlighted how such foundational elements enable emerging AI capabilities, including agentic systems, to deliver lasting value for investors. Wang's leadership at Vanguard focuses on advancing AI, machine learning, generative AI, and behavioral science to translate new technologies into trusted solutions that improve client experiences and business outcomes.

item.title: Blackstone says AI data center bottlenecks could boost value of existing facilities amid financing challenges and market uncertainties

Despite rising financing costs and challenges in the AI infrastructure sector, Blackstone reported strong leasing momentum and plans to continue investing heavily in AI ventures, including a joint venture with Google. Some AI-related companies face market difficulties, with CoreWeave's stock declining and Firmus and SB Energy considering or delaying IPOs amid broader market uncertainties.

item.title: US appeals court removes judge from Mississippi DEI ban case citing AI-related errors and lifts block on the ban
item.description: A US appeals court has removed a judge from a case involving Mississippi's ban on diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) policies due to errors related to artificial intelligence. The court also lifted the block on the state's DEI ban, allowing the policy to proceed. This decision highlights judicial scrutiny over AI's role in legal proceedings and impacts the enforcement of DEI regulations in Mississippi.

item.description: Anthropic reports that large language models (LLMs) are making formal software verification feasible on a much larger scale than before. This development could significantly improve the reliability and security of software systems by automating complex verification tasks. The company highlights how LLMs can assist in scaling formal methods, which traditionally require extensive manual effort and expertise, potentially transforming software development processes and reducing errors in critical applications.

item.title: OpenAI is working on a $30 billion funding round at a $1.25 trillion valuation ahead of its IPO [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI is reportedly close to securing a new $30 billion private funding round at a $1.25 trillion pre-money valuation, led by Coatue and investors from the UAE, as it prepares for an initial public offering. This valuation would make OpenAI the most highly valued private company ever, surpassing its previous $852 billion post-money valuation from March. The funding round may also include a deal to increase OpenAI's computing capacity from the UAE. OpenAI filed confidential IPO paperwork in June, and this new valuation could raise expectations for its public debut. The high valuation may also impact Anthropic's upcoming IPO, which is rumored to target a $1.5 to $2 trillion valuation following its own recent funding rounds and confidential filings.

item.title: Coverage Cat releases CATT 0.2.1 to test agents and services against Muse and Instinct emulation targets in continuous integration environments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Coverage Cat has released version 0.2.1 of the Consumer Agent Testing Tool (CATT), which allows developers to test how assistants interact with their services by running scripted or model-driven agents against MCP servers, apps, websites, or HTTP APIs. The tool supports Muse and Instinct surrogate emulation targets, enabling users to inspect service behavior, compare results across builds, and integrate testing into CI workflows. CATT requires Python 3.12 or newer, Node.js 20 or newer, and Chromium for browser lanes, with setup instructions provided for macOS and Linux environments. The tool includes features such as connector lane testing, readiness checks, and scripted runs, with some features relying on macOS-specific sandboxing. Documentation and quickstarts are available to help users test their own services and workflows.

item.title: Canva launches Craft, an AI image model that plans designs before generating images with up to 2K resolution and over 30 aspect ratios [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Canva has introduced Craft, its first in-house AI image generation model that uses a two-stage process to plan designs before creating images, aiming for greater precision and control. The model supports up to 2K resolution and more than 30 aspect ratios, enabling it to generate social media posts, marketing content, realistic scenes, and digital art with accurate text and object placement. Craft was trained on millions of human-made templates from Canva's content library and currently ranks fourth on Design Arena's AI image generation leaderboard. The company emphasizes robust moderation, privacy, and safety controls, and plans to integrate AI agents via the open Model Context Protocol. Craft is now available globally through Canva's Dream Lab feature.

item.title: Researchers and cybersecurity experts warn AI is accelerating discovery and exploitation of software vulnerabilities, with PHP2Shell exploits surging after AI-assisted discovery [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Cybersecurity experts and researchers have observed a rapid increase in the discovery and exploitation of software vulnerabilities powered by AI tools and large language models. Notably, the PHP2Shell vulnerability, found using AI by researchers from Wiz, Calif, and OpenAI, has seen millions of exploitation attempts within hours of public disclosure, highlighting AI's role in accelerating offensive hacking capabilities. Experts emphasize that AI is not sentient but is enabling hackers to efficiently identify and exploit weaknesses in widely used software, many of which were previously unnoticed or neglected. This shift is causing concern among security professionals, with some urging heightened defensive measures as AI fundamentally changes the cybersecurity landscape and the speed at which attacks can occur.

item.title: Phasefield.ai maps text surprise across a book using a fixed-memory language model to identify unusual passages and errors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Phasefield.ai applied a 12-million-parameter complex-valued language model with fixed-size state memory to analyze the text of Memoirs of the Court of Marie Antoinette, Volume 7, measuring the model's surprise at each byte to create a map of predictability across the book. The model highlighted dense lists of names, structural changes, and typing errors as peaks of unpredictability, while narrative prose was more predictable. This approach uses born attention to maintain constant memory usage regardless of text length, enabling efficient processing of large texts. The technique can flag transcription errors, unusual passages, and boilerplate, with potential applications in document ranking, compression, and anomaly detection in other data streams such as radio signals.

item.title: Liquid AI launches RIPL, a low-latency inference engine delivering under 50ms responses for real-time enterprise AI workloads [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Liquid AI announced RIPL (Real-time Inference Pipeline), a low-latency inference engine designed to deliver complete model responses in under 50 milliseconds even under peak traffic. RIPL targets real-time enterprise applications such as search rankings, product recommendations, fraud detection, and payment authorizations, where latency budgets are tight and traditional AI serving infrastructure is too slow. Shopify is deploying Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) with RIPL in production for latency-sensitive commerce workloads, achieving sub-20ms inference times and 2-10× faster performance compared to alternatives while using fewer parameters. RIPL supports NVIDIA GPUs like H100, H200, B200, and RTX PRO 6000 and is available for enterprise deployments requiring strict latency guarantees.

item.title: Salesforce Customers Brace For New Fees to Use Claude in Its Apps [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Salesforce is leading the software industry's attempt to collect fees from businesses that use Claude and other external AI tools to automate work in enterprise apps. As soon as next month, Salesforce plans to require companies to register outside AI agents, a step toward charging them each time those agents update or analyze data stored in Salesforce. The fees let Salesforce earn money from customers who use such AI instead of paying for Salesforce's built-in AI products. The Salesforce tollgate has implications for the rest of the industry, which is coming to terms with the idea that so-called AI agents may be able to use software firms' apps more efficiently than humans do, meaning their seat-based or per-user pricing model might not have staying power. The question is whether the new AI tollgates-which Atlassian, Workday, ServiceNow and Datadog are also erecting to various extents-and other pricing shifts will more than make up for an eventual decline in per-seat subscription revenues. The vast majority of workers haven't yet outsourced such work to AI, of course, and companies like Salesforce are trying to get more revenue from them as well. They charge fees based on how much they use the apps' built-in AI tools and are also experimenting with outcome-based pricing, meaning customers only pay when such tools actually complete a task successfully or help the customers make more money. For now, Salesforce and some other software firms developing tollgates for customers' AI agents haven't started charging the tolls. They're letting customers experiment for free with the technology a little while longer. (The customers still have to pay providers such as Anthropic to use the AI agents in the first place.) Starting around November, according to the company's website, Salesforce will require customers to register any externally-made AI agents if they plan to use them to take actions on their behalf in Salesforce apps. Each action an agent takes in Salesforce counts as a billable "interaction," according to the company. The move has lifted investor confidence in Salesforce recently. Salesforce describes the registration requirement as a security measure because the company gives each agent its own identity and narrower data-access permissions, compared to humans. It isn't clear how Salesforce will clamp down on customers using their own AI agents, such as OpenClaw-powered ones that run on a person's computer and can access any app that runs on it. (Salesforce did not respond to requests for comment.) Salesforce hasn't announced prices tied to such agent usage, but customers could eventually end up paying a lot more money than they do now, given how many of them are already using their own AI on top of Salesforce apps and bypassing Salesforce's own built-in AI tools, according to software consultants and chief information officers. Nick Hamm, a software consultant, said that most of the 150 enterprises he works with are currently using AI from Anthropic and OpenAI to automate work inside Salesforce apps, for free. But they're reconsidering that usage in anticipation of the upcoming fees. If the fees are too high, the customers may move their business data outside of Salesforce's apps so they can use AI to analyze the data without paying an extra cost, he said. New customers will have a three month grace period after the new pricing is announced to register their AI agents, and the pricing won't affect existing customers until their contracts are renewed. In addition to the billable "interactions," customers have the option to buy unlimited agent usage by purchasing a "headless license," a Salesforce account executive told Hamm in a LinkedIn message viewed by The Information. Some customers such as Lumen, a fiber-optic network provider to enterprises and data centers, say they are waiting to test Salesforce's new connectors until pricing is disclosed. So far, Lumen has leaned on Salesforce's built-in AI. A longtime customer of Salesforce's customer relationship management software, Lumen made a "major" investment in using Salesforce's AI sales agents in the last 12 months, according to CIO Jim Fowler. The sales agents help with tasks such as collecting customer information and generating sales quotes for the customers to buy fiber connections between data centers, saving Lumen's human salespeople considerable time, he said. So far, Fowler said, Salesforce has been "super flexible" about letting Lumen use existing subscription fees to also cover its use of built-in AI features such as the sales agents. Early customer reactions to the pricing announcement will likely determine how flexible Salesforce is with customers that start renewing their contracts after November. If its past AI pricing efforts are any guide, Salesforce could easily switch things up depending on the feedback, or any blowback, it receives. item.title: Utopai Becomes a Unicorn as Video AI Takes Off [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: While much of the AI industry has fixated on new personal AI assistants from Meta and OpenAI, video AI is enjoying a quiet renaissance. Hollywood mogul Jeffrey Katzenberg is teaming up with the former head of OpenAI's Sora app to launch a new AI film company. Startup Higgsfield quadrupled its valuation to $5.4 billion in August. And Kling AI, the video unit of Chinese social media giant Kuaishou Technology, raised nearly $3 billion at a $15 billion valuation over the summer. The latest video AI company to seize this moment is Utopai Studios, a 4-year-old film startup based in Mountain View, Calif. Utopai closed a funding round for $60 million that valued it at $1 billion and has already received term sheets for a subsequent round that would value the company at $2 billion to $3 billion, according to someone close to the company. The enthusiasm for video AI startups follows improvements in the quality and length of the clips that video AI models can generate. In September, Higgsfield announced that it had crossed $1 billion in annualized revenue, showing that the technology has serious commercial potential.

item.title: Only 13 percent of companies see real returns from AI, Gartner survey finds
item.description: Only 13 percent of companies are getting real business value from their AI investments, according to a Gartner survey of 2,002 CIOs. At the same time, 51 percent expect AI to actually increase their operating costs. Yet 75 percent of CEOs plan to keep raising their technology budgets.
